abstract: In mammals, embryogenesis normally unfolds within the uterus, limiting direct access to the developmental processes that transform a zygote into an embryo with forming organs. Although mouse embryos can be cultured ex utero from early post-implantation stages to mid-gestation, continuous culture from the zygote into organogenesis has not been achieved. Through comparative single-cell transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses, here we discover aberrant BMP signaling and suboptimal metabolic support as barriers to continuous ex utero development. BMP inhibition, together with stage-specific optimization of the culture environment, enables mouse zygotes to progress through peri-implantation development, gastrulation, and into early organogenesis ex utero. Cultured embryos form major embryonic and extraembryonic lineages, establish body axes, and generate multiple organ primordia, while retaining developmental delays and molecular differences from in vivo embryos. By connecting developmental stages that have previously been cultured separately, this study provides an accessible platform for dissecting how early mammalian development progresses into organ formation and a reference for evaluating stem-cell-based embryo models.
